analysis: Agent Memory Lab joined the matched cohort in a separate Actions run using the same sample and evaluation settings. It scored 1/3, found the annotated evidence session for all three questions, and used 231 MiB of sampled peak RAM. Its median search was 2.9 ms. The adapter ranks results from the native SQLite keyword lookup by the number of distinct query terms matched. The memory path used zero model tokens. The shared answerer and judge still made API calls.

The original ten frameworks and the BM25 control completed the same three questions. EverOS, Hindsight, Mem0 and MemOS scored 2/3. BM25, OpenSquilla, OpenViking, Cognee and Fraise scored 1/3. Graphiti and LangMem scored 0/3. Graphiti scored 2/3 on the previous run using the same sample, so a single three-question run gives an unstable ordering.

All candidates returned the annotated evidence sessions for the three questions. OpenSquilla, OpenViking and BM25 got the support-group date right, answered the sunrise question with “Last year” where the reference expected 2022, and gave an incomplete education answer. Session-level recall can succeed even when a particular turn, date or detail is missing from the answer.

OpenSquilla’s memory-only path indexed seven chunks from three sessions and used roughly 218 MiB of sampled RAM, compared with 680 MiB for OpenViking’s server and harness, and 176 MiB for BM25. OpenViking searched faster than OpenSquilla in this run (0.192 s versus 0.311 s median). These were four-vCPU runners with different CPU models across the matrix, so the timings describe the observed runs.

The repeat fixed GPT-6 sampling compatibility in EverOS and MemOS and set reasoning to none for LangMem’s function-tool calls. The quality run uses the RonsenbergVI harness with a fixed GPT-6 Luna reader and judge. OpenSquilla uses native session search, and OpenViking uses native session extraction plus dated transcript indexing.
